title: CJEU rules credit-bureau scoring can itself be prohibited automated decision-making under GDPR
description: On 7 December 2023, the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled in Case C-634/21 (OQ v Land Hessen) that when a credit reference agency such as SCHUFA Holding AG generates a probability score on a person's creditworthiness, and a third-party lender draws decisively on that score to decide a contract, this constitutes automated individual decision-making under GDPR Article 22(1) — even though the agency itself does not make the final lending decision. The case arose after a German loan applicant was refused a loan based on a SCHUFA score. The ruling was the CJEU's first interpretation of Article 22, and means Article 22 obligations can attach to a scoring intermediary, not only the final decision-maker.

history.note: Initial Edition 1.1 content, part of the shift to Phase 3 canonical knowledge expansion.

organizations_involved: Court of Justice of the European Union
root_cause: Ambiguity in GDPR Article 22 over whether an entity that only produces a recommendatory score, rather than the final contractual decision, engages in 'automated decision-making' — SCHUFA and lower German courts had previously read the provision narrowly to exclude scoring agencies.

citations.title: Judgment of the Court (First Chamber), 7 December 2023 — OQ v Land Hessen (SCHUFA Holding, Scoring), Case C-634/21
citations.publisher: Court of Justice of the European Union
citations.excerpt: Automated individual decision-making – Credit information agencies – Automated establishment of a probability value concerning the ability of a person to meet payment commitments in the future ('scoring') – Use of that probability value by third parties.

relationships.reason: A requirement that human reviewers genuinely deviate from a score, not rubber-stamp it, directly addresses the accountability gap this ruling closed.
This is the binding EU precedent establishing that a score alone can trigger Article 22 obligations.
